newsitem.title: USA: Powell has high popularity but no political plans.
newsitem.headline: Powell has high popularity but no political plans.

text.p: Popular retired Gen. Colin Powell, basking in the national spotlight as chair of the national summit on volunteerism, has made it clear in recent days he still does not foresee a political career.
Powell, who scored a 77 percent approval rating in the latest Gallup poll, with only seven percent disapproving, seems likely to go down in history as the William Tecumseh Sherman of his generation.

Sherman, a highly successful Civil War general, was hounded for years after his retirement from military life to run for president. His famous response: "If nominated, I will not accept. If elected, I will not serve."

Asked in a recent interview if he would repeat those words Powell said: "It would be not appropriate to plagiarise from General Sherman and to use such well-known words. But to use my own words, I'm very happy in private life and believe I'm making a significant contribution in private life."

The architect of U.S. military victory over Iraq in 1991 said he had not changed his mind since November 1995, when he decided not to seek the presidency. "It is now '97, nothing has changed. I don't expect to be entering political life. I don't have any plans for political office," he said on CNN.

That still may not quiet the speculation. In a Marist Institute poll of Republican voters published this week, Powell easily led the field of possible presidential nominees with 29 percent. Tying for second place, with 13 percent, were former Housing Secretary Jack Kemp and Texas Gov. George Bush.

Part of Powell's allure is his rags-to-riches story as the son of immigrants from the Caribbean who emerged from a New York City ghetto to become the first black chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff -- America's No. 1 military officer.

Retiring from the military in 1993, he wrote a wildly successful autobiography and criss-crossed the country promoting both it and himself. Then, in a dramatic news conference, he declared for the first time that he was a Republican and simultaneously withdrew himself from consideration for the presidency or the vice presidency.
He lacked the hunger and passion needed for political battle, he said. He also had to contend with strong opposition from his wife, Alma, who has battled depression for years.

Powell realises his current popularity stems from the fact that he is seen as being above politics and that much of that esteem would disappear if he entered the arena. "I am not in the hurly-burly of political life where I have to fight as politicians do hour after hour, day after day, creating enemies and allies on a rapidly changing basis," he said.
If he did seek political office, Powell would face stiff opposition from conservatives in the Republican Party who object to his support for abortion rights and suspect he is not really one of them.

Christian evangelicals comprise as much as 40 percent of Republican voters -- more in some states -- which is probably enough to deny the presidential nomination to any candidate they find objectionable.

Powell also appears happy with his life, which includes making $70,000 speeches, serving on the board of mainly black Howard University, the Boys and Girls Clubs of America, the Children's Health Fund and the College Fund. Now he has taken on the volunteerism project as well.

"I am in private life, and I was never a politician. I was a public servant as a soldier for 35 years. And just because I took off my uniform does not mean I instantly transformed myself into a political figure," Powell said.

"I don't think I have to be in political office to be influential. I think I can be influential in private life, which is where I've chosen to spend my time and to use whatever standing I have in the country."
